title: The star cluster NGC 3293
caption: The star cluster NGC 3293, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-meter telescope at La Silla
celestial: NGC 3293 · constellation Carina · about 8000 light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: Ranked #42 on ESO’s published “Top 100 Images” list (an institutional selection, not an audience score).

story: Young stars huddle together in this view, set against clouds of glowing gas and lanes of dust. This is the star cluster NGC 3293, photographed at ESO's La Silla Observatory in Chile by the MPG/ESO 2.2-meter telescope's Wide Field Imager.

The cluster was not always this bright group of stars. About ten million years ago it would have been only a cloud of gas and dust. As stars began to form inside that cloud, it turned into NGC 3293. In astronomical terms, that makes these stars youthful.

Clusters like NGC 3293 act as natural laboratories. Because their stars formed together from the same cloud at around the same time, they share a common starting point, which lets astronomers compare how stars of different masses change as they age.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (34.44 x 33.47 arcminutes) and distance (8000 light years), the frame spans roughly 80 × 78 light-years. Its light set out about 8,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This view comes from the Wide Field Imager, using B, V, I and hydrogen-alpha filters that span visible and near-infrared light. The color assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The near-infrared filter records light the eye cannot see, and the long exposures bring out faint glowing gas that would be invisible through an eyepiece.
